title: All is burning, read whole

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ananda corrected, and your line, walked with friends. Did you reach a good friend? Today we go back to a hilltop from year one and read the whole sermon spoken there. Day six hundred fifty-two.

A thousand men sit on a hill near Gaya. Until recently, every one of them tended sacred fires. They kept their hair matted and twisted, and they poured offerings into flames morning and night, under three brothers named Kassapa. Now they've become monks, followers of the Buddha. And the Buddha, standing on Gaya Head, gives them a sermon in a language they have lived inside for years. Fire. Year one told the story. Today we read the sermon itself, the way they heard it. Today: aditta.
screen: `A THOUSAND MEN ON GAYA HEAD.` → `ONCE, KEEPERS OF THE FIRE.` → `A SERMON IN THEIR LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: SN 35.28 opens: all is burning, monks. And what is the all that is burning? Then it walks through the senses, one by one, with a rhythm meant to be heard. The eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning. And whatever feeling arises from eye-contact, pleasant, painful or neither, that too is burning. Burning with what? With the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. Burning with birth, aging and death, with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair, I say. Then again for the ear and sounds. The nose and smells. The tongue and tastes. The body and touch. The mind and ideas. Six times the same pattern, until the whole world of experience is on fire. Then the turn. Seeing this, the well-taught disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with all of it. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are freed. And the text ends: while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of those thousand monks were freed from the taints. Notice what makes it work. It isn't a theory of fire. It's an image these men had lived inside for years. They knew how fire feeds on fuel and goes out when the fuel is gone. Buddhist teachers hear the same picture in the word nibbana: a fire going out. And the sermon ends the way a fire does, when nothing is left to feed it.
screen: `WHAT IS THE ALL THAT IS BURNING?` · `EYE, FORMS, CONTACT, FEELING` · `LUST, HATRED, DELUSION` · `DISENCHANTED, DISPASSIONATE, FREE` · then, large: `ALL IS BURNING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you're somewhere you can, read the sermon's pattern aloud, softly, at the pace of the breath. The eye is burning. Forms are burning. The ear is burning. Sounds are burning. The nose, smells. The tongue, tastes. The body, touch. The mind, ideas. Don't hurry it. Let each line land in the sense it names: look, listen, smell, taste, feel, think. Then sit quietly with whatever is left after the words stop. The bell holds the time.
aditta. The Pali word for burning, in the fire sermon of SN 35.28: the six senses, their objects and feelings, burning with lust, hatred and delusion, cooled by letting go. Today's word.
Your line: a little less fuel. Once today, when a sight or a sound sets you alight with wanting or irritation, notice the fire, and let it have a little less fuel. Day six hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: The Adittapariyaya Sutta, the fire sermon, is studied and chanted in many Theravada communities, and its pattern of the six senses is a common frame for meditation on sense experience.

myth: the fire sermon covers only the eye
it walks through all six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.
the monks who heard it had tended sacred fires
they were matted-hair fire ascetics under the three Kassapa brothers.
the thousand monks were freed while the sermon was still being spoken
the text says their minds were freed from the taints as they listened.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, about to teach a thousand men who've spent their lives tending sacred fires. what image do you use?
fork.reveal: he speaks in the language they know best: everything they experience is burning, and freedom is the fire going out.

original.note: Pali aditta: burning, on fire. SN 35.28 is the Adittapariyaya Sutta, the discourse on burning.

trapdoor: what you thought: all is burning is a warning about destruction.
what it means: in SN 35.28, the six senses, their objects and the feelings they bring are burning with lust, hatred and delusion, and letting go cools them.

what a scholar hears: the sermon belongs to the early story of the community at Gaya, told in the Vinaya's Mahavagga; scholars note how it speaks in the ritual language of fire to former fire-worshippers.

notes: SN 35.28 paraphrased; the practice reads a paraphrased refrain aloud rather than a fixed translation. A Keeper may wish to substitute an exact public-domain translation (e.g. Warren 1896 or Oldenberg and Rhys Davids' Vinaya Texts 1881) if one is approved.

Confirm the setting (Gayasisa, near Gaya, with a thousand bhikkhus, the former matted-hair ascetics under Uruvela, Nadi and Gaya Kassapa) and the ending (their minds were liberated from the taints by non-clinging).
'Western readers met it in the nineteenth century' is a soft claim; Eliot's 'The Fire Sermon' as section III of The Waste Land (1922) is well documented.
Year one (day 67) told the fire sermon story; this day reads it whole.

Softened 'the one language they know better than any other' and framed nibbana as a fire going out as how teachers hear it, not as an etymology.
